questions.e: A repair install fixes system files without wiping user data or apps. A clean install erases everything.

questions.q: Remote network installation of an OS requires the client to support what?
questions.e: PXE lets a NIC boot from the network and pull an OS image. It needs a DHCP server and deployment services such as WDS.

questions.q: During a Windows Server install, the setup can't see the disks attached to a RAID controller. What should the technician do?
o: Load the third-party RAID controller driver from USB during setup
questions.e: Some controllers need third-party drivers loaded during setup before the disks appear.

questions.q: What partition style and file system does a UEFI-bootable USB installer normally need?
questions.e: FAT32 is the key part: UEFI firmware can read FAT32, so it can boot from it. GPT is the partition style UEFI systems normally use, and it's what your notes give. Tools like Rufus or the Media Creation Tool set this up for you.

questions.q: A Mac has a blank drive and no USB installer. How can macOS be reinstalled?
o: PXE boot from a Windows server
questions.e: Internet-based installation downloads the OS from the vendor's servers; Apple's Internet Recovery does exactly this.

questions.q: A developer wants Windows 11 and Ubuntu on the same PC, choosing between them at startup. What is this called and what does it need?
o: Multiboot; separate partitions for each OS and a boot manager such as GRUB
questions.e: Multiboot (dual-boot) installs each OS on its own partition, with a boot menu (GRUB or Windows Boot Manager) to pick one.

questions.q: What is the maximum disk size supported by MBR?
questions.e: MBR tops out at 2 TB. GPT supports far larger disks (around 9.4 ZB).

questions.q: How many primary partitions can an MBR disk have?
questions.e: MBR allows 4 primary partitions. To get more, make one an extended partition containing logical partitions. GPT supports 128 partitions in Windows.

questions.q: Which partition style is required to install Windows 11 with UEFI and Secure Boot?
questions.e: GPT is required for UEFI boot. It also stores redundant partition tables with CRC32 checks, so it's more resilient than MBR.

questions.q: What is a logical partition?
o: A partition created inside an extended partition on an MBR disk
A partition that holds the GPT backup table
A partition only used by UEFI
questions.e: Logical partitions live inside an extended partition, letting MBR disks go beyond four partitions. They can't be marked active for booting.

questions.q: Which Windows feature is missing in Home edition, meaning administrators can't use gpedit.msc?
questions.e: Home lacks the Group Policy Editor; you'd have to make registry edits instead. Pro and Enterprise include it.

questions.q: What can a Windows 11 Home PC do with Remote Desktop?
o: Connect to other PCs as a client, but not host incoming sessions
Host sessions but not connect out
questions.e: Home can only act as an RDP client. Pro and Enterprise can host.

questions.q: What is missing from Windows 'N' editions sold in Europe?
o: Pre-installed media features like Windows Media Player
questions.e: N editions exclude media technologies. Users can add them with the Media Feature Pack.

questions.q: Which edition includes the Long-Term Servicing Channel (LTSC), suited to systems that must rarely change, like industrial or medical equipment?
questions.e: LTSC minimises feature updates for stability. It's an Enterprise option along with features like Credential Guard and AppLocker.

questions.q: Which Windows 10 edition adds ReFS support and up to 6 TB of RAM for high-end workstations?
questions.e: Pro for Workstations targets power users, adding ReFS and much higher RAM limits.

questions.q: A PC runs 32-bit Windows 10 and needs Windows 11 (64-bit only). Which approach is required?
o: A side-by-side upgrade on the same drive
questions.e: You can't upgrade in place from 32-bit to 64-bit. A clean install is required, after backing up data.

questions.q: An office is moving staff from old PCs to new ones and wants to keep each user's files and settings. Which method fits?
o: Side-by-side migration using a tool like USMT
questions.e: Side-by-side migration moves user data and settings from the old machine to the new one. User State Migration Tool (USMT) is the Microsoft tool for this.

questions.q: What is wipe-and-load migration?
o: Back up user data, wipe and reinstall the OS on the same machine, then restore the data
Copy settings from one PC to another
Boot the OS from the network each time
questions.e: Wipe-and-load gives a fresh OS on the same hardware with user data restored, so old problems don't carry over.

questions.q: Which upgrade method keeps the user's files, settings and installed apps?
questions.e: An in-place upgrade installs the new version over the old one, preserving files, settings and apps, as long as it's a supported upgrade path.

questions.q: What is the minimum RAM required for Windows 11?
questions.e: Windows 11 needs at least 4 GB RAM, 64 GB storage, a 1 GHz dual-core 64-bit CPU, TPM 2.0 and UEFI with Secure Boot.

questions.q: What is the minimum storage required for Windows 11?
questions.e: 64 GB is the minimum. Windows 10 64-bit needed only 20 GB.

questions.q: A Windows 10 PC fails the Windows 11 compatibility check. Which two firmware features are the most common reasons?
o: TPM 2.0 and UEFI with Secure Boot
questions.e: Windows 11 requires TPM 2.0 and UEFI Secure Boot. Older PCs often have them disabled, or lack TPM 2.0.

questions.q: What are the minimum RAM requirements for Windows 10?
questions.e: Windows 10 minimum is 1 GB (32-bit) or 2 GB (64-bit).

questions.q: A PC takes ages to boot. Which Task Manager tab lets you disable apps that launch at startup?
questions.e: The Startup tab lists startup apps with their impact (low, medium or high) and lets you disable them.

questions.q: Which Task Manager tab shows live graphs of CPU, memory, disk, network and GPU usage, plus system uptime?
questions.e: Performance shows real-time resource graphs and uptime. Processes breaks usage down per app/process.

questions.q: A browser has frozen. Where in Task Manager do you end it?
o: Processes tab, select it and End task
questions.e: The Processes tab lists running apps and background processes and lets you end unresponsive ones.

questions.q: On a shared PC, which Task Manager tab shows how much CPU and RAM each logged-in user is using?
questions.e: The Users tab shows logged-in users, their resource use, and lets you sign out inactive sessions.

questions.q: Which tool would you use to check system logs for critical errors before a crash?
questions.e: Event Viewer shows system, application and security logs.

questions.q: An external hard drive is connected but has no drive letter in File Explorer. Which tool fixes this?
questions.e: Disk Management manages partitions, formatting and drive letters.

questions.q: Which snap-in do you use to add a user to the local Administrators group?
questions.e: lusrmgr.msc creates and manages local accounts and group memberships.

questions.q: Which tool would you use to automatically run a cleanup script every Sunday at midnight?
questions.e: Task Scheduler automates tasks on a schedule or trigger.

questions.q: A laptop's webcam isn't working and you suspect a driver problem. Which tool shows the device and lets you update or roll back its driver?
questions.e: Device Manager shows hardware and drivers, with options to update, roll back, disable or uninstall.

questions.q: Which tool lets an administrator block USB storage or enforce password complexity on a Pro machine?
questions.e: Group Policy enforces security settings and restrictions.

questions.q: Which snap-in manages digital certificates used for encryption and authentication?
questions.e: Certificate Manager (certmgr.msc) is where you import, view and manage certificates.

questions.q: Which tool shows detailed hardware and software information, such as the BIOS version, CPU and installed RAM?
questions.e: msinfo32 gives a full system summary. It's handy for checking upgrade readiness or firmware versions.

questions.q: Which tool would you use to set Windows to boot into Safe Mode on the next restart?
questions.e: msconfig controls boot options, including Safe boot, and startup settings.

questions.q: A PC shows a low disk space warning. Which built-in tool removes temporary files and cached data?
questions.e: Disk Cleanup scans for and removes temporary and unnecessary files.

questions.q: Which tool gives a detailed live view of which processes are using disk I/O and network activity?
questions.e: Resource Monitor goes deeper than Task Manager, showing per-process CPU, memory, disk and network detail.

questions.q: Which tool gives direct access to edit Windows configuration settings stored in the registry?
questions.e: Registry Editor edits registry keys and values directly. Back up before changing anything.

questions.q: Which command scans for and repairs corrupted Windows system files?
questions.e: System File Checker repairs protected system files. chkdsk is for file system and disk errors.

questions.q: Which chkdsk switch locates bad sectors and recovers readable information?
questions.e: /f fixes file system errors. /r also finds bad sectors and recovers readable data (it implies /f).

questions.q: An admin has changed a Group Policy and wants it applied on a PC immediately. Which command?
questions.e: gpupdate /force refreshes policy straight away. gpresult shows which policies have been applied.

questions.q: A user complains a setting is locked. Which command shows which Group Policies are applied to them?
questions.e: gpresult /r lists applied policies. gpresult /h report.html creates a detailed HTML report.

questions.q: Which command mirrors a folder to a backup location, copying changes and removing files that no longer exist in the source?
questions.e: robocopy (Robust File Copy) is built for large and reliable copies. /mir mirrors the source to the destination.

questions.q: Which command opens a window showing the Windows version and build number?
questions.e: winver shows the version and build in a pop-up.

questions.q: Inside diskpart, which command shows all disks attached to the system?
questions.e: In diskpart, list disk shows the disks; select disk N chooses one; clean wipes its partitioning.

questions.q: Which command deletes a folder and all its subfolders?
questions.e: rmdir removes directories. /s includes all subdirectories and files, and /q stops it asking for confirmation. md creates directories.

questions.q: Which command formats drive E: as NTFS?
questions.e: format prepares a drive with a file system. /q does a quick format.

questions.q: A user wants to stop a particular app using their microphone. Where in Windows Settings should they look?
questions.e: Privacy (Privacy & security in Windows 11) controls app access to location, camera and microphone.

questions.q: A visually impaired user wants Windows to read on-screen text aloud. Which settings area has Narrator?
questions.e: Ease of Access includes Narrator, Magnifier and Sticky Keys.

questions.q: A user wants PDFs to open in Adobe Reader instead of Edge. Where do they change this?
questions.e: The Apps area manages installed apps and default app choices.

questions.q: Windows search is slow to find files in a folder the user uses a lot. Which Control Panel item can help?
questions.e: Indexing Options controls which locations Windows Search indexes for fast lookups.

questions.q: A networked app is blocked from accessing the network. Where would you create an exception?
questions.e: Windows Defender Firewall manages inbound and outbound rules and app exceptions.

questions.q: Which power state saves the session to disk and turns the PC fully off, using no power until it resumes?
questions.e: Hibernate writes RAM contents to disk and powers off completely. Sleep keeps the session in RAM using a little power for a quick resume.

questions.q: An external USB drive on a laptop keeps randomly disconnecting when idle. Which power setting should you disable?
questions.e: USB selective suspend puts idle USB devices into low power, which can make some drives drop out.

questions.q: What does Fast Startup do?
o: Saves system information to a hibernation file at shutdown to speed up the next boot
Keeps the PC in Sleep instead of shutting down
questions.e: Fast Startup is a hybrid shutdown that uses a hibernation file for quicker boots.

questions.q: A user on a long flight wants maximum laptop battery life. Which power plan suits them?
questions.e: Power Saver reduces CPU speed, dims the display and limits background activity.

questions.q: A user opened 'invoice.pdf.exe' thinking it was a PDF. Which File Explorer setting would help prevent this?
o: Turn off 'Hide extensions for known file types'
Open File Explorer to This PC
questions.e: With extensions hidden, 'invoice.pdf.exe' looks like 'invoice.pdf'. Showing extensions reveals disguised executables.

questions.q: A technician needs to reach application data stored in hidden folders like AppData. What should they enable?
o: Show hidden files, folders and drives
questions.e: Showing hidden files reveals folders like AppData that are hidden by default.

questions.q: Which directory service stores user accounts, computers and policies centrally in a Windows domain?
questions.e: Active Directory is the directory service on the domain controller. Group Policy is the set of rules applied through it.

questions.q: A family has three PCs at home and wants to share files and a printer. Which setup is appropriate?
questions.e: Workgroups are peer-to-peer, decentralised and suit small networks. Each PC manages its own accounts.

questions.q: In a workgroup, where are user accounts managed?
questions.e: Workgroups have decentralised administration, so each PC has its own accounts and sharing permissions.

questions.q: Which macOS file type is a disk image you mount and then drag the app from into /Applications?
questions.e: .dmg is a disk image. .pkg is an installer package that runs automated installation. .app is the application bundle itself.

questions.q: Which macOS folder holds user-specific preferences and caches, where deleting a corrupted cache can fix a crashing app?
questions.e: Each user's ~/Library holds their app data and caches. /Library is system-wide, and /System holds core OS files that shouldn't be touched.

questions.q: What is macOS's built-in backup tool?
questions.e: Time Machine makes automatic backup snapshots. FileVault is encryption, Keychain is a password manager and Spotlight is search.

questions.q: What is Rapid Security Response on macOS?
o: Fast-tracked security patches delivered between major OS updates
questions.e: RSR delivers urgent security fixes quickly without waiting for a full update.

questions.q: Which macOS feature securely stores passwords, certificates and Wi-Fi keys?
questions.e: Keychain is the built-in password manager. You can look up a saved Wi-Fi password in Keychain Access.

questions.q: Which macOS feature provides full-disk encryption?
questions.e: FileVault is Apple's disk encryption, the Mac equivalent of BitLocker.

questions.q: Which keyboard shortcut opens Force Quit on a Mac?
questions.e: Command + Option + Esc opens the Force Quit window for unresponsive apps.

questions.q: A user copies text on their iPhone and pastes it on their Mac. Which macOS feature makes this possible?
questions.e: Continuity covers Handoff, Universal Clipboard and AirDrop across Apple devices.

questions.q: Which macOS tool can repair a corrupted external drive using First Aid?
questions.e: Disk Utility manages, formats, partitions and repairs disks.

questions.q: Which macOS feature gives an overview of all open windows and desktops at once?
questions.e: Mission Control shows all windows and desktops. It's often opened with a three-finger swipe up.

questions.q: Which Linux file stores encrypted (hashed) user passwords?
questions.e: /etc/shadow holds password hashes and policies. /etc/passwd holds account info like usernames, UIDs and home directories.

questions.q: Which Linux file defines which drives are mounted automatically, and where, at boot?
questions.e: /etc/fstab lists file systems and mount points for persistent mounts.

questions.q: Which file holds the DNS server addresses a Linux machine uses?
questions.e: /etc/resolv.conf stores DNS servers. /etc/hosts maps hostnames to IPs locally.

questions.q: A developer wants testsite.local to resolve to 127.0.0.1 on their Linux machine only. Which file should they edit?
questions.e: /etc/hosts gives local name-to-IP mappings that override DNS.

questions.q: Which Linux component manages services and the boot process on modern distributions, controlled with systemctl?
questions.e: systemd manages boot, services and logging. GRUB is the bootloader, Bash is a shell, and root is the superuser account.

questions.q: What is GRUB?
o: A Linux bootloader that loads the OS and can present a dual-boot menu
questions.e: GRUB (and the older LILO) are bootloaders.

questions.q: What is the difference between su and sudo?
o: su switches to another user (often root); sudo runs a single command with elevated privileges
sudo switches user permanently; su runs one command
su installs software; sudo removes it
questions.e: su switches user accounts. sudo grants temporary admin rights for one command, which is safer than staying logged in as root.

questions.q: Which Linux command gives a script execute permission?
questions.e: chmod changes permissions. chown changes ownership.

questions.q: Which command searches a log file for lines containing 'error'?
questions.e: grep searches inside files for text patterns. find searches for files by name, size or date.

questions.q: Which package manager do Red Hat-based distributions like Fedora use?
questions.e: dnf replaced yum on Red Hat-based distros. apt is the Debian/Ubuntu package manager.

questions.q: Which command shows free and used space on mounted file systems?
questions.e: df shows disk free space per file system. du shows how much space directories and files use.

questions.q: Which Linux command gives a live, Task Manager-style view of processes and CPU/memory usage?
questions.e: top updates in real time. ps gives a one-off list of running processes.

questions.q: Which command shows the current directory you're working in?
questions.e: pwd prints the working directory. ls lists its contents.

questions.q: Which command opens the manual page for chmod?
questions.e: man displays manual pages for commands.

questions.q: Which command renames oldlog.txt to newlog.txt?
questions.e: mv moves or renames. cp would leave the original in place.

questions.q: Which statement about 32-bit and 64-bit applications is correct?
o: 32-bit apps can run on a 64-bit OS, but 64-bit apps need a 64-bit OS and CPU
questions.e: 64-bit Windows runs 32-bit apps fine (through WOW64), but 64-bit apps need a 64-bit OS.

questions.q: What is the difference between dedicated and integrated graphics?
o: Dedicated graphics have their own VRAM; integrated graphics share system RAM
Dedicated graphics are built into the CPU
questions.e: Dedicated GPUs have their own VRAM and suit 3D, CAD and video work. Integrated graphics borrow system memory.

questions.q: A VPN app requires users to plug in a USB key to authenticate. What kind of requirement is this?
questions.e: Some applications need security tokens or dongles, often for MFA or licensing.

questions.q: A large software rollout is scheduled overnight so it doesn't slow the office network during the day. Which impact consideration is this?
questions.e: Large downloads eat bandwidth, so scheduling off-peak reduces the network impact.

questions.q: How can you install software from an ISO file without burning it to a disc?
o: Mount the ISO as a virtual drive
Copy it to the Startup folder
questions.e: ISO files can be mounted as virtual drives (double-click in Windows, or a .dmg-style mount on macOS) and installed like physical media.

questions.q: What is a Type 1 hypervisor?
o: A bare-metal hypervisor that runs directly on the hardware, with no host OS
A hypervisor that runs as an application on top of a host OS
A container engine that shares the host kernel
questions.e: Type 1 (bare-metal) examples: VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V, XenServer. Type 2 (hosted) runs on a host OS: VMware Workstation, VirtualBox, Parallels.

questions.q: A student wants to try Linux inside a VM on their Windows laptop using free software they install like any other app. Which is the best fit?
questions.e: VirtualBox is a Type 2 hypervisor: easy to install on an existing OS and ideal for end users.

questions.q: How do containers differ from virtual machines?
o: Containers share the host OS kernel and isolate just the app and its dependencies, so they are lighter and start faster
Containers each run a full guest OS
Containers can't be moved between environments
questions.e: Containers (Docker, Kubernetes) are lightweight and portable because they don't carry a whole OS. VMs virtualise full hardware and run a complete guest OS.

questions.q: A security analyst wants to run a suspicious file safely to see what it does. What is the main VM purpose here?
questions.e: A sandbox is an isolated environment where untrusted software can run without affecting the host.

questions.q: An accounting package only runs on Windows XP. How can the business keep using it on modern hardware?
o: Run Windows XP in a VM (legacy software/OS virtualisation)
Install it on Windows 11 in compatibility mode only
Run it in a public cloud SaaS
questions.e: VMs let legacy OSs and apps run on modern hardware. The notes' scenario does exactly this. Keep such VMs isolated as they no longer get security updates.

questions.q: What is VDI?
o: Virtual Desktop Infrastructure: desktops hosted centrally on servers and accessed from any device
A virtual hard disk file format
questions.e: VDI centralises desktops on servers, giving remote access, central management and lower client hardware costs.

questions.q: Which is a networking requirement for virtual machines?
o: Virtual switches, virtual network adapters and VLANs
A dedicated physical NIC per VM in every case
questions.e: VMs connect to physical and virtual networks through virtual switches and adapters, with VLANs used to separate traffic.

questions.q: When creating a Hyper-V VM for a modern OS that supports UEFI and Secure Boot, which generation should you choose?
questions.e: Generation 2 supports UEFI and Secure Boot. Generation 1 is for older operating systems.

questions.q: What is the Hyper-V option that lets the host adjust a VM's RAM up and down as needed?
questions.e: Dynamic Memory lets Hyper-V change a VM's memory allocation dynamically. Startup memory is what it gets at boot.

questions.q: Which file format does Hyper-V use for new virtual hard disks by default?
questions.e: Hyper-V uses VHD/VHDX virtual disks (VHDX is the newer default). .iso files are used as installation media to attach to the VM.

questions.q: Several hospitals share cloud infrastructure built to meet the same healthcare compliance rules. Which cloud deployment model is this?
questions.e: A community cloud is shared by organisations with common requirements, such as compliance.

questions.q: A company keeps sensitive data in its own private cloud but runs its public website on a public cloud. Which model is this?
questions.e: Hybrid combines private and public cloud, with integration between them.

questions.q: A company uses Microsoft 365 for email and documents and doesn't manage any servers. Which service model is this?
questions.e: Software as a Service delivers ready-to-use applications. The provider manages everything underneath.

questions.q: A start-up rents virtual servers, storage and networking from a cloud provider and installs and manages its own OS and apps. Which service model is this?
questions.e: Infrastructure as a Service provides raw virtualised resources. The customer manages the OS and everything above it.

questions.q: Developers deploy their code to a managed platform (like AWS Elastic Beanstalk) without managing servers or the OS. Which service model is this?
questions.e: Platform as a Service gives developers a platform and tools to build and deploy apps while the provider manages the infrastructure.

questions.q: An online shop's cloud resources automatically scale up for Black Friday traffic and back down afterwards. Which characteristic is this?
questions.e: Elasticity is scaling resources up or down dynamically with demand.

questions.q: What does multitenancy mean in cloud computing?
o: One instance of a service is used by many customers, each with isolated data
questions.e: Multitenancy lets many customers (tenants) share the same platform with their data kept separate.

questions.q: In cloud billing, what is egress?
o: Data transferred out of the cloud
The number of tenants on a server
questions.e: Ingress is data in; egress is data out. Note: your notes say ingress costs more, but in practice it's the other way round: major providers usually charge for egress and make ingress free or cheap. Watch out for this on the exam.

questions.q: What is metered utilisation?
o: Tracking resource use and charging based on consumption
A fixed monthly fee regardless of use
Limiting a laptop's data on a mobile hotspot
Splitting one server between many tenants
questions.e: Metered utilisation means paying for what you use, which also enables chargeback to the departments responsible.

questions.q: A user's laptop is running out of space because OneDrive is downloading a huge archive folder. What should you configure?
o: Selective sync (sync/folder settings) to keep only needed folders locally
Change the OneDrive licence to SaaS
questions.e: Sync/folder settings let users choose which folders sync to each device, while the rest stays online.

questions.q: A company wants staff accounts in Slack to match their Azure AD (Entra ID) accounts automatically. What is this called?
questions.e: Identity synchronisation keeps user profiles and permissions consistent across multiple tools.

questions.q: An admin gives managers a higher tier of Teams subscription with longer meeting limits than other staff. What is this?
questions.e: Licence assignment gives users access levels based on their role and the subscription plans available.

questions.q: Which is an advantage of cloud-based email systems like Microsoft 365?
o: No on-premises mail servers to maintain, and access from any device
They work without an internet connection
questions.e: Cloud email is delivered over the internet, so there are no local mail servers to run and mail, calendar and contacts sync across devices.

questions.q: What is an access control vestibule (formerly called a mantrap)?
o: A secure entryway with two doors that lets only one person through at a time after authentication
A post that stops vehicles getting close to a building
A device that scans employee badges
A camera system that records entrances
questions.e: Vestibules stop tailgating by holding one person between two doors until they're authenticated. Bollards are the vehicle posts.

questions.q: A bank wants to stop vehicles being driven into its front entrance. Which control fits?
questions.e: Bollards are vertical posts that block vehicle access to entrances and critical infrastructure.

questions.q: A school wants to stop classroom laptops being stolen while still letting students use them. Which control fits best?
questions.e: Equipment locks, such as cable locks, physically tie devices down.

questions.q: How does good perimeter lighting improve security?
o: It deters intruders and makes video surveillance more effective
questions.e: Lighting removes dark areas, deterring intruders and helping both guards and cameras.

questions.q: Which device detects concealed metal objects such as weapons at a building entrance?
questions.e: Magnetometers use electromagnetic fields to detect metal, as at security checkpoints.

questions.q: Which access method uses a phone or smartwatch, typically via NFC or Bluetooth, in place of a physical key?
questions.e: Mobile digital keys turn a phone or watch into the key, such as a hotel room key on your phone.

questions.q: Which biometric method scans the pattern of blood vessels at the back of the eye?
questions.e: Retina scanners use infrared to map retinal blood vessels. They're high-security and used in places like government facilities.

questions.q: Which card has an embedded chip storing authentication credentials and is inserted into or tapped on a reader?
questions.e: Smart cards store credentials on a chip and are often used to log into laptops as well as open doors.

questions.q: A database admin can manage databases but can't change system files outside that role. Which principle is this?
questions.e: Least privilege means giving only the minimum access needed to do the job.

questions.q: Which security model assumes no implicit trust and continuously verifies every user, device and app, even inside the network?
questions.e: Zero Trust means never trust, always verify, regardless of where a request comes from.

questions.q: A student logs in once and gets access to email, course materials and the finance portal without signing in again. What is this?
questions.e: SSO lets you authenticate once for multiple services. SAML is a protocol often used to make web-based SSO work.

questions.q: Which protocol exchanges security assertions so users can sign into cloud web apps using their corporate credentials?
questions.e: Security Assertion Markup Language enables SSO across web applications.

questions.q: An admin is granted elevated rights to a server only for the length of a troubleshooting task, after which they're automatically removed. What is this?
questions.e: JIT access gives temporary elevated privileges and revokes them afterwards, shrinking the window for misuse.

questions.q: A company wants to stop staff uploading confidential files to personal cloud storage. Which technology does this?
questions.e: DLP blocks unauthorised data transfers and accidental leaks.

questions.q: What is a TOTP?
o: A time-based one-time password that changes at fixed intervals, often generated by an authenticator app
questions.e: TOTP codes regenerate every 30 seconds or so using a shared secret and the current time.

questions.q: Which solution controls and monitors administrator and other high-privilege accounts, such as requiring approval before use?
questions.e: PAM limits and audits privileged account use to cut the risk of breaches.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a form of multifactor authentication described in the notes?
o: Asking the user to type the same password twice
questions.e: MFA combines different factors. Entering the same password twice is still just one factor (something you know).

questions.q: What is implicit deny on a firewall?
o: Traffic is blocked by default unless a rule explicitly allows it
A specific rule blocks a known bad IP address
All traffic is allowed unless blocked
questions.e: Implicit deny is the default block. Explicit deny is a specific rule you write to block something.

questions.q: Teams can't connect through the Windows firewall on a user's PC. What is the simplest fix?
o: Allow the app through the firewall (create an app exception)
questions.e: Allowing a trusted app creates an exception without weakening protection for everything else.

questions.q: Which tool gives fine-grained control of ports, programs, IP ranges and connection security rules (IPsec)?
o: Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security
The Windows Security app's simple toggle
questions.e: The Advanced Security console (wf.msc) handles detailed inbound/outbound rules and IPsec connection security.

questions.q: What is the difference between inbound and outbound firewall rules?
o: Inbound controls traffic coming into the PC; outbound controls traffic leaving it
Inbound is for Wi-Fi; outbound is for Ethernet
Inbound is for apps; outbound is for ports
questions.e: Inbound rules filter incoming connections; outbound rules filter connections the PC makes.

questions.q: What can a standard user account NOT do?
o: Install software or make system-wide changes
Save files in their own profile
questions.e: Standard accounts can use apps and personal settings but need admin approval to install software or change the system.

questions.q: What does User Account Control (UAC) do?
o: Prompts for administrator approval before system changes are made
questions.e: UAC asks for consent or admin credentials before elevated actions, which helps stop malware and accidental changes.

questions.q: Which group can back up and restore files even without explicit permissions on those files?
questions.e: Backup Operators have special rights to back up and restore regardless of file permissions.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of a Microsoft account over a local account?
o: Settings, files and apps sync across devices through the cloud
It works without any internet ever
questions.e: Local accounts live only on the device. Microsoft accounts are cloud-based and sync across devices.

questions.q: A technician needs to run a command that changes system settings. How should they open Command Prompt?
o: Right-click and choose Run as administrator
Open it as the Guest user
Open it in Safe Mode only
Open it from the Startup folder
questions.e: Run as administrator launches the program with elevated privileges (after a UAC prompt).

questions.q: A user has Full Control NTFS permission on a folder but only Read share permission. What can they do when accessing it over the network?
o: Only read, because the most restrictive of NTFS and share permissions applies
Full control, because NTFS overrides share
questions.e: Over the network, both apply and the most restrictive wins. Locally, only NTFS permissions apply.

questions.q: Which statement about share permissions is correct?
o: They only apply when a folder is accessed over the network
They apply to local and network access
They are more granular than NTFS permissions
questions.e: Share permissions (Read, Change, Full Control) only affect network access. NTFS permissions are more granular and apply locally and over the network.

questions.q: Which NTFS permission lets users read, write, run and delete files, but not change permissions or take ownership?
questions.e: Modify covers read, write, execute and delete. Full Control adds changing permissions and taking ownership.

questions.q: By default, what happens to permissions when a new file is created in a folder?
o: It inherits the parent folder's permissions
It gets Full Control for Everyone
It copies the permissions of the last file edited
questions.e: Inheritance is on by default. You can disable it, but then you have to set permissions manually.

questions.q: Which tool shows the actual combined permissions a user has once NTFS, share and group memberships are all taken into account?
questions.e: The Effective Access tab works out the real result of all the permissions that apply to a user.

questions.q: Which file attribute does backup software use to tell which files have changed and need backing up?
questions.e: The Archive attribute flags new or modified files for backup.

questions.q: What is an Organisational Unit (OU) in Active Directory?
o: A container used to group users and computers so different policies can be applied
A type of security group for file shares
questions.e: OUs organise AD objects. Moving a user to a different OU can change which Group Policies apply to them.

questions.q: A user logs into a different office PC and wants their Desktop and Documents to be there. Which AD feature provides this?
questions.e: Folder redirection moves profile folders like Desktop and Documents to a network location, available from any domain PC.

questions.q: Network drives should map automatically for every user at sign-in. What is the usual way to do this in a domain?
o: Assign a login script (via Group Policy or the user's AD properties)
questions.e: Login scripts run at sign-in to map drives, set variables and similar tasks.

questions.q: What is a home folder in Active Directory?
o: A private network storage location assigned to each user
A shared folder for a whole department
questions.e: A home folder is a per-user private drive on a file server, set in the user's AD properties.

questions.q: What does BitLocker use to securely store its encryption keys on the PC?
questions.e: BitLocker is full-disk encryption that relies on the TPM chip to protect keys.

questions.q: An employee needs to encrypt a USB stick of confidential reports before posting it to another office. Which Windows feature fits?
questions.e: BitLocker To Go encrypts removable drives using a password or smart card.

questions.q: Which Windows feature encrypts individual files and folders on NTFS for a specific user account, rather than the whole drive?
questions.e: EFS is file-level encryption tied to the user's account. BitLocker encrypts the whole volume.

questions.q: What is cipher text?
o: Data that has been encrypted and can't be read without the key
A type of password hash list
questions.e: Plain text is readable; cipher text is the encrypted, unreadable form.

questions.q: Which Wi-Fi security protocol is the most secure, with stronger protection against brute-force and dictionary attacks?
questions.e: WPA3 improves on WPA2 with stronger encryption, brute-force resistance and forward secrecy. WEP and TKIP are obsolete and insecure.

questions.q: Which encryption algorithm do WPA2 and WPA3 use?
questions.e: AES is the strong modern algorithm. TKIP was a stopgap used by original WPA and is now considered weak.

questions.q: Why should WPS be disabled on a router?
o: Its PIN method can be brute-forced to gain access
questions.e: Wi-Fi Protected Setup's PIN-based pairing is vulnerable to brute-force attacks.

questions.q: Staff connect to corporate Wi-Fi with their own usernames and passwords, checked by a central server. Which authentication service is typical?
questions.e: RADIUS centralises network access authentication, as used with WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise.

questions.q: Which authentication protocol was developed by Cisco and encrypts the whole authentication process, giving granular control over admin access to network devices?
questions.e: TACACS+ encrypts the entire exchange and separates authentication, authorisation and accounting, which makes it popular for managing network devices.

questions.q: Which ticket-based protocol do Windows domain controllers use to authenticate users?
questions.e: Kerberos uses tickets so users can authenticate to services securely over an untrusted network.

questions.q: Which malware disguises itself as legitimate software but gives attackers access when it runs?
questions.e: Trojans pretend to be useful programs. Worms spread on their own; viruses attach to files.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a virus and a worm?
o: A worm spreads across networks on its own; a virus needs a host file and user action to spread
A virus spreads on its own; a worm needs a user
questions.e: Viruses attach to files and spread when executed. Worms self-propagate across networks, often through unpatched vulnerabilities.

questions.q: Which malware hides deep in the OS to keep long-term privileged access while avoiding detection?
questions.e: Rootkits embed themselves at a low level and can hide from normal security tools. Removal may need a reinstall.

questions.q: A PC is slow and its CPU fan is always loud. You find a process using 100% CPU that mines cryptocurrency. What is this?
questions.e: Cryptominers hijack system resources to mine cryptocurrency without consent.

questions.q: Which malware runs only in memory, for example through PowerShell, leaving few or no files on disk?
questions.e: Fileless malware lives in memory and abuses legitimate tools, which makes it hard to detect with file-based scanning.

questions.q: Which type of malware infects the master boot record so a PC may not start?
questions.e: Boot sector viruses infect the MBR and are hard to remove. A recovery environment is often needed.

questions.q: Which is spyware used to secretly track a person's location, messages and calls, often for personal surveillance?
questions.e: Stalkerware is a form of spyware aimed at monitoring a specific person.

questions.q: A free game installed an unwanted browser toolbar that slows the PC. It isn't strictly malicious. What is it most likely to be?
questions.e: PUPs often come bundled with free software: toolbars, trackers, bloatware.

questions.q: What is the difference between EDR and MDR?
o: EDR is a tool monitoring endpoints; MDR is a managed third-party service providing monitoring and response
EDR is outsourced; MDR is a tool
questions.e: Endpoint Detection and Response is the technology on devices. Managed Detection and Response is a service with experts monitoring 24/7.

questions.q: Which solution correlates data from endpoints, network, email and cloud for wider threat visibility?
questions.e: XDR combines data from multiple security layers into one view with automated response.

questions.q: A company wants to block phishing emails and malicious attachments before they reach inboxes. What should it deploy?
questions.e: Email security gateways filter inbound and outbound mail for phishing, spam and malware.

questions.q: What is the last-resort method for guaranteeing malware removal?
questions.e: Formatting and reinstalling (or reimaging) removes everything, so it's used when an infection like a rootkit can't be trusted to be cleaned.

questions.q: Which human-focused measure most reduces the success of phishing?
questions.e: User education, such as phishing awareness training and simulations, tackles the human weakness phishing relies on.

questions.q: A caller claiming to be from the bank's fraud team asks a customer to confirm their card details. What type of attack is this?
questions.e: Vishing is voice phishing over the phone. Smishing is by SMS.

questions.q: A CEO receives a convincing, personalised fake legal notice by email asking for confidential documents. What type of attack is this?
questions.e: Whaling is spear phishing aimed at high-profile people such as executives.

questions.q: Someone follows an employee through a secure door without swiping their own badge. What is this?
questions.e: Tailgating means slipping in behind an authorised person. Access control vestibules and security awareness help prevent it.

questions.q: An attacker searches a company's bins for printed reports and old drives. What is this?
questions.e: Dumpster diving targets discarded material, so shredding and proper data destruction matter.

questions.q: A fake parking meter sticker sends people to a malicious site when they scan it. What is this attack?
questions.e: QR code phishing uses malicious codes to send victims to credential-stealing or malware sites.

questions.q: How does spear phishing differ from ordinary phishing?
o: It targets a specific person or organisation with personalised details
It is always done by phone
It is sent to millions of random addresses
questions.e: Spear phishing is targeted and personalised. Whaling is spear phishing aimed specifically at senior executives.

questions.q: An attacker sets up a Wi-Fi hotspot called 'Airport_Free_WiFi' that looks like the real one, to capture logins. What is this?
questions.e: An evil twin is a rogue access point pretending to be a legitimate network.

questions.q: What is the difference between a DoS and a DDoS attack?
o: DDoS uses many compromised systems (a botnet) to flood the target
DoS uses a botnet; DDoS uses one machine
questions.e: Both overwhelm a target with traffic. Distributed DoS comes from many sources, which makes it harder to block.

questions.q: An attacker types database commands into a website's login box and pulls out user records. What is this?
questions.e: SQL injection inserts malicious SQL into queries. XSS injects scripts that run in other users' browsers.

questions.q: An attack exploits a software flaw that the vendor doesn't yet know about and has no patch for. What is it called?
questions.e: Zero-day means the defenders have had zero days to fix it.

questions.q: How is a dictionary attack different from a basic brute-force attack?
o: It uses a list of common words and leaked passwords rather than trying every combination
questions.e: A dictionary attack is a smarter brute force using likely passwords. Long, unique passwords and lockout policies help defend against both.

questions.q: Finance staff receive an email that appears to come from the CEO, urgently asking for a bank transfer to a new supplier account. What is this?
questions.e: BEC impersonates executives or partners to trick staff into payments or data disclosure. Verify requests by another channel.

questions.q: Attackers compromise a trusted software vendor's update so thousands of customers install malware. What type of attack is this?
questions.e: Supply chain attacks get in through a trusted third party.

questions.q: Which attack intercepts, and may alter, traffic between two parties without them knowing?
questions.e: On-path attacks sit between victim and destination, for example on public Wi-Fi.

questions.q: Staff connect personal laptops with no company security controls to the network. Which vulnerability is this, and what helps?
questions.e: Bring Your Own Device introduces devices without enterprise security. MDM lets you enforce settings on them.

questions.q: What is the difference between a vulnerability and an exploit?
o: A vulnerability is a weakness; an exploit is the technique or code that takes advantage of it
An exploit is a weakness; a vulnerability is the attack
A vulnerability only applies to people
questions.e: The vulnerability is the hole; the exploit is how an attacker uses it.

questions.q: A database was left publicly reachable because of a wrongly configured firewall rule. Which vulnerability type is this?
questions.e: Default credentials, unnecessary open ports and bad permissions are misconfigurations. Regular audits and secure baselines help.

questions.q: What is the FIRST step in the CompTIA malware removal process?
questions.e: Start by confirming it really is malware. Note: your notes list five steps, but the official CompTIA order has seven: 1) investigate and verify, 2) quarantine infected systems, 3) disable System Restore (Windows Home), 4) remediate, 5) schedule scans and run updates, 6) enable System Restore and create a restore point, 7) educate the end user.

questions.q: In the official CompTIA malware removal process, what comes straight after verifying the symptoms?
questions.e: Quarantine (isolate it from the network and stop sharing media) so it can't spread. Your notes leave this step out, but it's in the official objectives.

questions.q: Why is System Restore disabled during malware removal on Windows Home?
o: Restore points may contain the malware and could reinfect the system
It speeds up the antivirus scan
It's needed to boot into Safe Mode
questions.e: Infected restore points could bring the malware back. Turn it off before cleaning and back on afterwards.

questions.q: Why should you update anti-malware definitions before scanning an infected PC?
o: So the scanner can detect the newest threats
questions.e: Out-of-date definitions may miss the very malware you're trying to remove.

questions.q: Malware keeps reloading every time Windows starts, stopping the scanner from removing it. What should you try?
o: Scan in Safe Mode or from a preinstallation environment (WinPE)
questions.e: Safe Mode loads minimal drivers so the malware doesn't run. WinPE scans from outside the infected OS completely.

questions.q: Malware has been removed and scans are now scheduled. What should be done before handing the PC back?
o: Re-enable System Restore, create a clean restore point and educate the user
questions.e: The final steps are re-enabling System Restore with a fresh restore point, then educating the user so it doesn't happen again (the last step is in the official objectives, not your notes).

questions.q: What is the difference between data-at-rest and data-in-transit encryption?
o: At rest protects stored data (e.g. BitLocker); in transit protects data moving across networks (e.g. TLS, VPN)
At rest is for networks; in transit is for drives
In transit only applies to USB drives
questions.e: BitLocker covers data at rest. TLS/HTTPS and VPNs cover data in transit.

questions.q: Which account policy defends against brute-force password guessing?
o: Lock the account after a number of failed attempts
questions.e: Failed-attempt lockout stops attackers trying endless passwords.

questions.q: A contractor needs network access for a three-month project. Which account setting ensures the account stops working when the project ends?
questions.e: Account expiration dates disable temporary accounts automatically.

questions.q: Which hardening step stops malware launching automatically from an inserted USB stick?
questions.e: AutoRun can execute code from removable media as soon as it's inserted. Disabling it removes that risk.

questions.q: Why rename the default Administrator account and set a strong password on it?
o: Attackers know the default name, so renaming makes it harder to target
questions.e: Changing the default admin account and password is a standard hardening technique.

questions.q: What is the best way for a user to handle lots of strong, unique passwords?
o: Write them on sticky notes under the keyboard
Use the same strong password everywhere
Save them in a text file on the desktop
questions.e: Password managers store and generate complex passwords securely, avoiding reuse.

questions.q: Which method uses a strong magnetic field to erase data on magnetic media such as HDDs and tapes?
questions.e: Degaussing destroys magnetic data. It doesn't work on SSDs or flash media, which aren't magnetic.

questions.q: A user formats a USB drive before selling it. Is the data gone?
o: No, a standard format removes file system structures but data can often be recovered
questions.e: Standard formatting isn't secure erasure. Use wiping/overwriting tools, or physical destruction for sensitive data.

questions.q: A company has an outside firm destroy its old drives. What document proves the job was done properly?
questions.e: Certified vendors provide a certificate of destruction as proof for compliance.

questions.q: A school wants to reuse old hard drives in student PCs. Which approach is appropriate?
o: Securely wipe/erase the drives so they can be reused
questions.e: Wiping (overwriting) allows reuse. Shredding, incineration and degaussing destroy the drives (degaussing ruins an HDD for reuse).

questions.q: What is the first thing you should change on a new SOHO router?
questions.e: Default credentials are widely published online. Changing them is the top priority.

questions.q: Why disable UPnP on a SOHO router?
o: It lets devices and malware open ports automatically without approval
questions.e: Universal Plug and Play is convenient but can be abused to open ports silently.

questions.q: A small business runs a public web server and wants it separated from internal systems. Where should it go?
o: On the same VLAN as the finance PCs
questions.e: A screened subnet isolates public-facing services from the internal network.

questions.q: A café wants customers on Wi-Fi without access to the till system. What should be set up?
o: Disable SSID broadcast on the main network only
questions.e: Guest access gives an isolated network for visitors with no route to internal devices.

questions.q: Which router feature lets an external user reach a specific internal service, such as a VPN server, through the firewall?
questions.e: Port forwarding maps an external port to an internal device and port.

questions.q: What does disabling SSID broadcast achieve?
o: It hides the network name from casual view, though it isn't strong security on its own
It turns off the 2.4 GHz band
questions.e: Hiding the SSID only stops casual discovery. Strong encryption (WPA3, or WPA2 with AES) is what actually protects the network.

questions.q: How can you confirm a downloaded browser installer hasn't been tampered with?
o: Compare its hash (e.g. SHA-256) with the one published by the developer
Run it in private browsing mode
questions.e: Hashing verifies integrity. If the hashes match, the file is identical to the one the vendor published.

questions.q: What does Secure DNS (DNS over HTTPS) do in a browser?
o: Encrypts DNS lookups to stop tracking and DNS spoofing
questions.e: DoH and DoT encrypt DNS queries, stopping ISPs and attackers seeing or tampering with them.

questions.q: Where should browser extensions be installed from?
o: Official stores such as the Chrome Web Store or Firefox Add-ons
questions.e: Untrusted extensions can steal data, inject ads or act as spyware. Also watch out for extensions asking for excessive permissions.

questions.q: What does private browsing mode do?
o: Stops the browser saving history, cookies and form data for that session
Encrypts all your traffic like a VPN
Hides your IP address from websites
questions.e: Private mode keeps the session out of local history, but it doesn't hide you from websites, your employer or your ISP.

questions.q: A user types google.com but lands on an unfamiliar search page. Which causes should you check?
o: Malicious extensions, changed DNS settings or a tampered hosts file
questions.e: Redirection comes from browser hijackers, compromised DNS settings or malware editing the hosts file.

questions.q: A user's files all have a strange new extension and won't open, and a note demands Bitcoin. What has happened?
questions.e: Renamed, encrypted files plus a ransom note mean ransomware. Isolate the PC immediately and restore from clean backups.

questions.q: A user gets a certificate warning when logging into their bank on a public network. What is a possible cause?
o: An on-path (MITM) attack intercepting the connection
questions.e: Certificate warnings can mean expired or revoked certificates, misconfiguration or interception. Don't proceed on a banking site.

questions.q: A PC repeatedly fails to install Windows security updates and antivirus keeps getting turned off. What should you suspect?
o: Malware such as a rootkit interfering with update and security services
questions.e: Malware often disables security tools and blocks updates to protect itself.

questions.q: A pop-up says 'Your PC has 37 viruses! Pay £39.99 to clean now' from software the user didn't install. What is this?
questions.e: False antivirus alerts come from scareware trying to get money. Remove the rogue program and scan with trusted tools.

questions.q: A company-wide email outage stops several departments working. Which severity level should the ticket get?
questions.e: Critical means business-critical systems are down for many users. High is a major loss of function (e.g. email down for one department), Medium is degraded with a workaround, and Low is minor or cosmetic.

questions.q: Network speeds are slow but staff can still work. Which severity fits best?
questions.e: Medium is degraded performance with workarounds available.

questions.q: Which support tier normally handles password resets and basic software installs?
questions.e: Tier 1 is basic support. Tier 2 handles network, advanced software and hardware issues. Tier 3 handles system-wide failures, deep OS problems and security. Management gets involved for compliance, legal or critical service issues.

questions.q: Why should a technician record each troubleshooting step in the ticket's progress notes?
o: So anyone picking up an escalated ticket can see what's been tried and doesn't repeat it
So the user can close the ticket themselves
It replaces the need for an issue resolution
questions.e: Progress notes log steps, attempted fixes and results. Clear written communication also covers the issue description and the final resolution.

questions.q: Which detail belongs in the device information section of a ticket?
o: Model, serial number, OS version, installed updates and network settings
The user's job title and manager
questions.e: Device information gives the technical context. User information covers name, department, contact details, device ownership and permissions.

questions.q: Which database stores detailed information about hardware, software and network configurations, helping identify changes that caused problems?
questions.e: A CMDB is a central repository of configuration items and their details.

questions.q: A technician scans a sticker on a laptop to see its history and warranty status. What is the sticker?
questions.e: Asset tags and IDs uniquely identify assets for tracking.

questions.q: What does the procurement life cycle track?
o: The acquisition, use and retirement of IT assets
Who a ticket is assigned to
questions.e: Procurement life cycle covers the whole life of an asset from purchase to disposal.

questions.q: Before replacing a failing drive, what should a technician check in the asset records?
o: Warranty information, as it might be covered by the manufacturer
questions.e: Warranty and licensing records show whether repairs or replacements are covered.

questions.q: An employee is leaving. Which document ensures their accounts are disabled, access revoked and devices returned?
questions.e: Off-boarding checklists stop leftover access and data leaks when someone leaves.

questions.q: An agreement with an ISP guarantees 99.9% uptime and set response times. What is it?
questions.e: SLAs define service levels. Internal SLAs are between IT and other departments; external SLAs are with outside providers.

questions.q: Which document gives step-by-step instructions so a task (like a password reset) is done the same way every time?
questions.e: SOPs ensure consistency and help train new staff.

questions.q: After a ransomware attack, the admin writes up affected systems, response actions and mitigation. What is this document?
questions.e: Incident reports support root cause analysis, trend spotting and compliance audits.

questions.q: A help desk publishes a step-by-step guide on setting up work email on phones to cut calls. Where would this live?
questions.e: Knowledge bases hold troubleshooting guides, how-to articles and FAQs for staff and users.

questions.q: Which type of change is pre-approved and low risk, like routine antivirus definition updates?
questions.e: Standard changes follow routine, pre-approved procedures. Normal changes need formal review and approval. Emergency changes are made immediately and documented afterwards.

questions.q: A server is under active attack and needs an urgent patch right now. Which change type applies?
questions.e: Emergency changes fix critical threats or outages immediately and are documented retrospectively.

questions.q: A retailer stops all non-essential IT changes during the Christmas shopping season. What is this called?
questions.e: A change freeze halts non-essential changes during critical periods. A maintenance window is a pre-set time slot for doing changes.

questions.q: What is a rollback plan?
o: A predefined way to return systems to their previous working state if a change goes wrong
A full backup of user data
questions.e: Rollback plans let you undo a failed change quickly. Backups protect the data itself.

questions.q: Who reviews and approves proposed changes before they are implemented?
questions.e: The change board checks changes against business objectives and risk before approving them.

questions.q: Before rolling out an HR software update to everyone, a developer tests it in an isolated environment. What is this?
questions.e: Sandbox testing catches problems before they hit production.

questions.q: After a new email security tool is deployed, staff are asked to confirm their email still works properly. Which step is this?
questions.e: End-user acceptance confirms the change meets expectations and hasn't broken anything.

questions.q: Which backup type copies only data changed since the last backup of any type, and clears the archive bit?
questions.e: Incremental backups are quickest to take and smallest, but a restore needs the full backup plus every incremental since.

questions.q: A full backup runs on Sunday with differentials Monday to Friday. The server dies on Thursday. Which backups are needed to restore?
o: Sunday's full and every differential since
questions.e: Each differential contains all changes since the last full, so you only need the full plus the most recent differential.

questions.q: What is a synthetic full backup?
o: A full backup built by merging the last full with later incrementals, without re-reading all the source data
A backup of only system files
A copy stored in the cloud
questions.e: Synthetic fulls reduce load on production systems while still giving you a complete restore point.

questions.q: What does the 3-2-1 backup rule say?
o: 3 copies of data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy offsite
3 backups a day, 2 a week, 1 a month
Keep backups for 3 years, 2 months and 1 day
questions.e: 3 copies (production plus two backups), 2 media types, 1 offsite.

questions.q: In the grandfather-father-son rotation, what does the 'father' represent?
questions.e: Son is daily, father is weekly and grandfather is monthly.

questions.q: After a ransomware attack, IT wants to check restored files are clean before putting them back into production. Which recovery method should it use?
o: Delete and re-download from the internet
questions.e: Restoring to an alternative location avoids overwriting current data and allows checking first.

questions.q: Why should backups be tested regularly?
o: To make sure the data can actually be restored when needed
questions.e: An untested backup may turn out to be corrupt or incomplete just when you need it.

questions.q: Where should an ESD wrist strap be clipped?
o: To an unpainted metal part of the chassis or a grounded workstation
To the CPU heatsink fins only
It doesn't need to be connected
questions.e: The strap grounds you so static doesn't discharge into components. It must connect to bare, grounded metal.

questions.q: Before replacing a PSU, what should a technician do?
o: Unplug the PC and press the power button to discharge remaining power
Leave it plugged in so it stays grounded
Put on safety goggles and work with it running
questions.e: Disconnect power first to remove shock and short-circuit risk. Never open a PSU itself.

questions.q: A technician is replacing a toner cartridge in a laser printer. What personal protection is recommended?
o: An air filter mask to avoid breathing in fine toner particles
questions.e: Toner is a very fine powder, so the notes recommend an air filter mask.

questions.q: Which fire extinguisher class does CompTIA say to use on electrical fires?
questions.e: In the US system the exam uses, Class C is for electrical fires. Heads-up for the UK: here 'Class C' means flammable gases, and you'd use a CO2 extinguisher on electrical fires. For the exam, answer Class C.

questions.q: How should a 25 kg UPS be moved?
o: Use a trolley/cart, or lift with knees bent and back straight
Lift quickly with a bent back
Drag it by its power cable
Carry it alone above head height
questions.e: Use proper lifting technique, and lifting equipment for heavy loads.

questions.q: How should spare RAM modules be stored?
o: In antistatic bags, handled by the edges
Wrapped in a plastic carrier bag
questions.e: Antistatic bags protect components from ESD during storage and transport.

questions.q: Which document explains how to safely handle, store and dispose of a hazardous material such as a battery or toner?
questions.e: SDS (formerly MSDS) documents give handling and disposal instructions for hazardous materials.

questions.q: What is the recommended humidity range for IT equipment rooms?
questions.e: Too dry increases static (ESD) risk; too humid causes condensation and corrosion.

questions.q: What is a brownout?
questions.e: A brownout is a sag in voltage; a surge is a spike; a blackout is complete loss of power.

questions.q: Which device provides battery backup so a server can shut down safely during a power cut?
questions.e: An uninterruptible power supply gives temporary power. Some include AVR to smooth out voltage. Surge protectors only stop spikes.

questions.q: What does a surge protector's joule rating tell you?
o: How much energy it can absorb before it fails
How long it can run on battery
questions.e: Higher joule ratings mean more surge energy can be absorbed.

questions.q: How should old laptop lithium-ion batteries be disposed of?
o: Through approved e-waste/battery recycling following local regulations
questions.e: Batteries contain toxic materials and are a fire risk. Recycle them through approved schemes.

questions.q: What should be used to remove dust from inside a PC?
o: Compressed air or an ESD-safe vacuum
A damp cloth on the motherboard
questions.e: Normal vacuums can generate static. Use compressed air or ESD-safe vacuums.

questions.q: Investigators record every person who handles a seized laptop, and when. What is this record called?
questions.e: Chain of custody documents handling of evidence so it stays admissible.

questions.q: According to the order of volatility, which should be collected first?
questions.e: Collect the most volatile data first (memory, cache), because it's lost when power goes or over time.

questions.q: Why do forensic investigators make a bit-by-bit copy of a drive?
o: To preserve the original evidence unchanged while they analyse the copy
questions.e: A forensic image protects data integrity. Analysis happens on the copy.

questions.q: What is a perpetual licence?
o: A one-time purchase that allows indefinite use, though updates may not be included
A licence for personal use only
questions.e: Perpetual licences are bought once. Subscriptions are recurring. Open source (GPL, MIT, Apache) allows free use and modification under conditions.

questions.q: Which standard governs the handling of credit card payment data?
questions.e: PCI DSS covers card data. HIPAA covers US healthcare data. GDPR covers personal data in the UK/EU.

questions.q: Which document must employees agree to that defines acceptable and unacceptable use of company IT resources?
questions.e: The AUP sets the rules for using company systems and networks.

questions.q: A contractor must agree not to share confidential source code they'll see. Which agreement covers this?
questions.e: NDAs prevent sharing confidential information. A mutual NDA (MNDA) binds both parties.

questions.q: A login screen reminds users that access is monitored and only authorised use is allowed. What is this?
questions.e: Splash screens display compliance or legal notices before system access.

questions.q: A technician is running 15 minutes late for an onsite visit. What should they do?
o: Contact the customer to let them know
questions.e: Be on time, and if you're late, contact the customer.

questions.q: Which question best clarifies a vague report that 'email doesn't work'?
o: "Are you unable to send emails, receive them, or both?"
"Have you tried turning it off and on again?" only
questions.e: Open, clarifying questions and restating the issue help narrow the scope without being judgemental.

questions.q: A customer is frustrated and blames IT for a problem they caused. What is the best approach?
o: Stay calm, don't argue or get defensive, and focus on fixing the problem
Explain firmly that it's their own fault
questions.e: Don't argue, don't be defensive, don't dismiss or judge. Keep the focus on the solution.

questions.q: While fixing a user's PC you notice confidential documents open on the desk. What should you do?
o: Leave them alone and respect the user's privacy
Read them in case they relate to the fault
questions.e: Handle customers' confidential and private materials appropriately, whether on screen, on the desk or at the printer.

questions.q: What should a technician do after resolving an issue, to complete good customer service?
o: Document the work and follow up later to confirm the user is satisfied
Close the ticket immediately with no notes
Tell the user to call back if it breaks again
Ask the user to write the documentation
questions.e: Provide documentation of the services and follow up to verify satisfaction.

questions.q: When explaining a fix to a non-technical user, what should you avoid?
questions.e: Plain language helps users understand what's happened and what they need to do.

questions.q: Which file extension is a Windows PowerShell script?
questions.e: .ps1 is PowerShell, .bat is a Windows batch file, .sh is a Linux/Unix shell script and .vbs is VBScript.

questions.q: Which script type would a Linux admin most likely use to automate weekly log cleanup?
questions.e: Shell scripts (.sh) run commands in Bash, Zsh and similar shells on Linux/Unix.

questions.q: Which is a risk when running scripts?
o: A badly vetted script could introduce malware or change system settings unexpectedly
questions.e: Risks include introducing malware, changing settings unintentionally and crashes from mishandled resources (e.g. infinite loops). Test scripts in a sandbox first.

questions.q: Which scripting language is cross-platform and widely used for automation, data analysis and networking tasks?
questions.e: Python runs on Windows, macOS and Linux and has extensive libraries.

questions.q: A JavaScript auto-refresh function loops endlessly and the browser hits 100% CPU. Which scripting consideration does this illustrate?
o: Browser or system crashes from mishandling resources
questions.e: Inefficient or infinite-loop scripts can overload resources.

questions.q: Which remote access tool is cross-platform, uses the RFB protocol and has no built-in encryption, so it should be tunnelled over SSH or a VPN?
questions.e: VNC works on Windows, macOS and Linux. RDP is Microsoft's protocol on port 3389.

questions.q: How should RDP be secured?
o: Restrict it to internal networks or a VPN, use MFA, and disable it when not needed
questions.e: Exposed RDP is a common target for brute-force attacks.

questions.q: What are best practices for securing SSH?
o: Use key-based authentication, disable root login and block repeated failed attempts (e.g. fail2ban)
Allow root login with a simple password
questions.e: SSH (port 22) is encrypted, but it still needs hardening against brute force.

questions.q: A managed service provider uses one platform to monitor clients' PCs, push patches and fix problems remotely. What is this?
questions.e: RMM tools let MSPs monitor, patch and manage endpoints at scale.

questions.q: Which Windows service allows remote execution of PowerShell commands using WS-Management?
questions.e: Windows Remote Management should use HTTPS, be restricted to admins and be disabled where it isn't needed.

questions.q: Which remote protocol is optimised for accessing virtual machines, commonly with KVM on Linux?
questions.e: SPICE (Simple Protocol for Independent Computing Environments) gives high-performance graphical access to VMs.

questions.q: Which secure protocols should file transfer software use?
questions.e: SFTP and FTPS encrypt transfers. Plain FTP sends data and credentials in clear text.

questions.q: An AI chatbot confidently tells a customer about a refund policy that doesn't exist. Which AI limitation is this?
questions.e: Hallucinations are false or misleading output presented as fact.

questions.q: An AI recruitment tool favours candidates from certain backgrounds because of its training data. Which limitation is this?
questions.e: Bias comes from unbalanced or incomplete training data and can lead to unfair decisions.

questions.q: Why might a company choose a private AI model over a public one?
o: Better control of data security and privacy, and training on its own relevant data
Public models are always more accurate
Public models can't be used for chat
questions.e: Private models keep sensitive data in-house and can be trained on company data. Public tools are general and may not protect confidential inputs.

questions.q: A company policy says AI-generated content must be checked and properly attributed by a human. Which policy concern does this address?
questions.e: AI policies cover appropriate use and plagiarism, requiring human verification and citations.

questions.q: What is the first step of the CompTIA troubleshooting methodology?
o: Establish a theory of probable cause
questions.e: The six steps: 1) identify the problem, 2) establish a theory of probable cause (question the obvious), 3) test the theory, 4) establish a plan of action and implement the solution, 5) verify full functionality and implement preventive measures, 6) document findings, actions and outcomes.

questions.q: Which step comes immediately after 'establish a theory of probable cause'?
o: Test the theory to determine the cause
questions.e: Theory, then test. If the test doesn't confirm it, form a new theory or escalate.

questions.q: Your test shows your theory was wrong. What should you do next?
o: Establish a new theory, or escalate
questions.e: If the theory isn't confirmed, go back to step 2 and form a new one, or escalate if you can't.

questions.q: What is the final step of the troubleshooting methodology?
o: Document findings, lessons learned, actions and outcomes
questions.e: Documentation is last so future technicians can resolve similar problems faster.

questions.q: During 'identify the problem', what should you do before making any changes to the user's system?
o: Gather information, ask about recent changes, and back up data if applicable
questions.e: Talk to the user, check error messages and logs, find out what changed and, where appropriate, back up data first.

questions.q: A user's laptop won't connect to Wi-Fi. The technician first checks whether the Wi-Fi switch or Airplane Mode is on. Which principle is this?
o: Question the obvious when establishing a theory
questions.e: Establishing a theory starts with the simplest, most common causes before complex ones.

questions.q: After fixing an issue, a technician checks everything works, confirms with the user and recommends preventive steps. Which step is this?
o: Verify full system functionality and implement preventive measures
questions.e: Step 5: make sure it's fully fixed and doesn't come back.

questions.q: What does ECC RAM do?
o: Detects and corrects single-bit memory errors, so it's used in servers
Lets DDR4 fit in a DDR5 slot
questions.e: Error-correcting code memory catches and fixes memory errors. Servers and workstations use it for stability, and the motherboard and CPU must support it.

questions.q: Can a DDR4 DIMM be installed in a DDR5 motherboard slot?
o: No, the notch position differs so the generations aren't interchangeable
Yes, but it runs at DDR5 speed
questions.e: Each DDR generation is keyed differently and electrically incompatible. Always match the RAM type to the motherboard.

questions.q: A PC has four DIMM slots colour-coded in pairs. To get dual-channel performance with two sticks, how should they be installed?
o: In matching slots of the same colour (per the motherboard manual)
Both in adjacent slots of different colours
In any two slots, as it makes no difference
One stick in each of two different PCs
questions.e: Multi-channel memory (dual, triple, quad) needs modules installed in the right matched slots, ideally with identical modules.

questions.q: How many pins does a desktop DDR4 or DDR5 DIMM have?
questions.e: Desktop DDR4 and DDR5 DIMMs both have 288 pins but different notch positions. DDR3 DIMMs have 240. Laptop SO-DIMMs: DDR3 204, DDR4 260, DDR5 262.

questions.q: Which form factor of RAM is used in most laptops that have upgradeable memory?
questions.e: SO-DIMM (small outline DIMM) is the compact laptop form factor. DIMMs are for desktops.

questions.q: A traveller wants to add a mobile data plan to their phone without inserting a physical SIM. What makes this possible?
questions.e: An eSIM is an embedded, programmable SIM that can be activated from carrier details or a QR code.
questions.l: Mobile connectivity and app support (thin in your notes)

questions.q: A company lets staff use their own phones for work email but wants to manage only the work apps and data, not the whole device. Which approach fits?
o: Mobile application management (MAM) or a work profile under MDM
questions.e: For BYOD, organisations often manage just the corporate apps and data (MAM / work profiles), while corporate-owned devices are fully managed with MDM.
questions.l: Mobile connectivity and app support (thin in your notes)

questions.q: A new phone is set up with a Microsoft 365 account. Which data types typically sync?
questions.e: Mobile account setup (Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, iCloud) syncs mail, calendar and contacts, and often cloud files too.
questions.l: Mobile connectivity and app support (thin in your notes)

questions.q: Which technology lets a phone's maps app pinpoint its location most precisely outdoors?
questions.e: Location services combine GPS (most precise outdoors) with cellular and Wi-Fi location. Users can restrict location access per app.
questions.l: Mobile connectivity and app support (thin in your notes)

questions.q: A user with a small monthly data cap keeps running out because photos back up to the cloud over mobile data. What should you change?
o: Set cloud backup/sync to work over Wi-Fi only
Switch from eSIM to physical SIM
questions.e: Sync settings should account for data caps. Restrict large syncs to Wi-Fi.
questions.l: Mobile connectivity and app support (thin in your notes)

questions.q: A company phone is lost on a train. Which two features help most?
o: A locator app to find it and remote wipe to erase it
questions.e: Locator apps track a lost device; remote wipe removes data if it can't be recovered. Both are typically enforced through MDM.
questions.l: Securing mobile devices (not in your notes)

questions.q: Which screen lock type is generally the weakest?
questions.e: A swipe lock gives no real authentication. PINs, patterns and biometrics all require something from the user.
questions.l: Securing mobile devices (not in your notes)

questions.q: What does a 'failed login attempts restriction' do on a phone?
o: Locks the device, adds delays, or wipes it after too many wrong attempts
Stops the phone connecting to Wi-Fi
questions.e: This protects against brute-force guessing of PINs and passcodes.
questions.l: Securing mobile devices (not in your notes)

questions.q: How can a company push consistent security settings (Wi-Fi, VPN, passcode rules) to many phones?
o: Manually texting each user the settings
questions.e: MDM configuration profiles enforce settings across corporate and BYOD devices.
questions.l: Securing mobile devices (not in your notes)

questions.q: Which is a key difference between BYOD and corporate-owned devices from a security point of view?
o: BYOD devices belong to the user, so policies must balance company data security with personal privacy
BYOD devices are always more secure
